source.title: A More Practical Approach to Machine Unlearning

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. It contains some internal inconsistencies, including different perplexity values in Table 4 and section 9.1.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies gradient-ascent unlearning and measures changes in tracked influence scores, but does not test the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports influence-score changes and layer-specific gradient-unlearning outcomes. It does not measure targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance or test recovery through fine-tuning, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompting. Perplexity and ROUGE results are not recovery-attack tests.
record.test_reason: This is a GPT-2 gradient-ascent unlearning method paper on 20 fictional sentences. It reports only its own influence scores, ROUGE and perplexity. It runs no recovery attack (fine-tuning, ablation, quantization, prompting) and no chance-level targeted-accuracy test. It neither tests nor relies on the shallow-unlearning finding and only cites Eldan & Russinovich. The record's tests/T2 should be cites_only/T6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that first-epoch gradient ascent reduced target influence and changed outputs, and that embedding-only gradients match whole-model gradients at about half the memory. They also judge first-epoch gradients more effective than multi-epoch ones. They concede it is unclear whether the effect is significant versus baseline or amounts to certified removal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses stored, per-data-point gradients and a custom fictional-character dataset with GPT-2; reports influence scores and layer-restricted unlearning rather than the listed LLM unlearning recipes or recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Unlearning outcome varies with the layer gradients used: layers 11 and 12 alone were ineffective, while including or using embedding layer 0 changed outputs or removed data points. The paper also discusses differences by unlearning duration.

fits_no_version.finding: During continued gradient-ascent iterations, influence scores for a target point fall and then rise after about 100 iterations. ROUGE on Dave also partly recovers around 210-260 iterations. This is spontaneous, not an attack.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over-long gradient-ascent unlearning can drift back toward the forgotten data without any relearning attack.

fits_no_version.finding: Perplexity on the Dave forget set stays near 1.1-1.45 after unlearning, against 29129 before fine-tuning, while ROUGE falls from 0.61 to about 0.17-0.28.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Surface-generation metrics can indicate forgetting while likelihood of the forgotten text remains high.

fits_no_version.finding: Paired t-tests on influence scores, and the layer-specific results showing embedding-layer gradients needed while layers 11-12 alone are ineffective.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this GPT-2 gradient-ascent setup, the unlearning effect depends on including embedding-layer gradients.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to GPT-2 and a custom dataset of 20 fictional-character statements. The study does not run the claimed recovery attacks or test chance-level targeted accuracy. The meaning and direction of the signed influence scores are not fully clear from the reported descriptive table. Perplexity figures differ between Table 4 and section 9.1.
record.rows_left_out: Perplexity and ROUGE results were not extracted as rows because they do not test any listed recovery mechanism or measure targeted accuracy against chance; the text reports these in sections 4.5, 4.7, and 9.1. Generated-text examples in Table 2 likewise are not recovery attacks.

untested.parts: No targeted accuracy versus chance, no separate general-ability benchmark, no attacks.
No relearning fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation. No analysis separating blocked access from deletion; the layer-restricted gradient results are not this.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context recovery tests.
No robustness claim or test against recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The perplexity values in Table 4 and section 9.1 are inconsistent. The perplexity is measured on the forget (Dave) dataset itself, so it is not a general-ability check. Single author, preprint, tiny synthetic dataset.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure targeted accuracy against chance, general ability on a separate task, or whether simple attacks recover knowledge.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning attack using unrelated, loosely related, or subset-of-facts examples.
No activation-direction ablation and no analysis distinguishing blocked access from deletion.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, alternate-language, or in-context-information recovery test.
No method is tested for resistance to the listed recovery attacks.

relation.reason: It cites Eldan & Russinovich (an original) only in related work, plus a one-line remark that gradient ascent gives incomplete forgetting. It does not test or use the shallow-unlearning finding. The reader's earlier tests/T2 call is not supported.

tranche.reason: GPT-2 gradient-ascent unlearning on 20 fictional sentences, measured by influence score, ROUGE and perplexity. It has no recovery attack, no targeted-accuracy-to-chance test and no claim of resisting attacks, so it neither tests nor uses any version.

source_check.notes: All 10 rows match the text. Table 1 differences are measured against Before Fine-Tuning, so they show residual distance, not reduction. The unlearned means in Table 3 (-1009, -1032) lie between finetuned (-1905) and baseline (-541). Table 1 and Table 3 don't reconcile: Table 3 baseline minus model-unlearning is 467.81, which is Table 1's 'Embedding' value. Perplexity on the Dave data stays about 1.1-1.45 after unlearning (Table 4).
